q8.answer: Each customer's count lives in a Redis counter keyed rl:<customerId>:<minute>, so all six gateway instances read and write the same number. Old counts are removed by Redis expiry: each key expires 60 seconds after it is written.

q9.answer: The budget does not drain back gradually. Because the counter key includes floor(unixSeconds / 60), a new minute produces a new key starting from zero, so each customer gets a fresh budget at each minute boundary.

q10.answer: The check and the increment run as one Lua script inside Redis, which runs it without any other command in the middle. The script increments only when the count is below the limit, so two instances cannot both take the last slot.

q11.answer: The script reads Redis TIME and returns the seconds until the next minute boundary, and the gateway sends that value rounded up with a minimum of 1. It deliberately does not use the counter key's expiry, since that can differ from the real reset point.

q12.answer: The design does not say whether the gateway retries the store; I never decided that, so the retry part is open. What the client gets is decided: on store error or timeout the request is forwarded with no X-RateLimit-Limit or X-RateLimit-Remaining headers, and the open question of whether any rate-limit header should appear on a fail-open response is listed as unresolved in the document.
